_comment: Every hook here runs on the PINNED runtime the client installs, not on whatever `node` is on
PATH. ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/runtime/node is ONE path that works on all three platforms: it is
extensionless, and a raw process start on Windows resolves it to node.exe (measured on
10.0.26200). See RUNTIME_INTERPRETER in @granthiaai/shared for why it sits at the runtime root
rather than under bin/ - it is a migration decision, not a stylistic one.
EXEC FORM (`command` plus `args`) rather than one shell string, everywhere it is available. No
shell parses these, so a path containing a space or a quote cannot break them, and - the part
that matters on Windows - there is no bash-vs-PowerShell question. Claude Code picks the shell
for a shell-form hook based on whether that machine has Git Bash, so the same string would get
different interpreters on two Windows boxes.
THE ONE EXCEPTION is provision-runtime, which stays on PATH `node` on purpose. It is the hook
that CREATES the pinned interpreter; pointing it at that interpreter would be circular, would
brick every existing install the moment the plugin updated, and could never install a runtime
on a machine that has none. It is the bootstrap. Safe because the installer is now fatal when
it cannot provision, so a machine with no Node never reaches a session with no runtime.
It is also the one hook left in SHELL form. Exec form is a raw process start, and on Windows that
resolves an extensionless name through .com and .exe ONLY - so a node.cmd or node.bat PATH shim,
which scoop and some corporate installs use, would not start it. Shell form recovers that case
WHERE POWERSHELL IS THE SHELL. It does NOT recover it under Git Bash, which Claude Code prefers
when present and whose execvp appends the same .exe/.com and no more - so Windows + Git Bash + a
.cmd shim remains a machine this hook cannot start on. Shell form is strictly better here and is
not a complete answer; the complete answer is the installer, which is why it is now fatal.
Every other hook names an absolute path and so does not care; this one searches PATH, and it is
the hook that must run for a machine to repair itself at all.
WHICH IS WHY THERE ARE TWO OF THEM. A PATH-`node` bootstrap cannot run on a machine that has no
Node - and that machine is not hypothetical, it is the one this whole feature exists for. Phase
1's installer needs no interpreter (curl and tar), so a macOS or Linux developer with no Node
ran it successfully and has runtime/bin/node with no canonical name. On update, every pinned
hook here would fail and the PATH bootstrap could never run to repair it: bricked, silently,
with the developer given no reason to re-run an installer.
The second bootstrap names runtime/bin/node directly, which is exactly what that population
has. It is not circular, because it is not trying to CREATE a runtime - it repairs one that is
already there. On Windows that path does not exist (the zip puts node.exe at the runtime root)
so the hook simply fails to start, which is harmless: Windows needs no repair, its node.exe
already satisfies the extensionless canonical name. A log line on Windows is a cheap price for
not bricking every bare POSIX machine.
